field_notes: Long streaming blue tail, black hood, yellow bill. Loud and conspicuous in pairs/groups.
Small, orange-red bill, yellow-orange throat, olive back. Noisy flocks in scrub.
Bright orange-yellow with silver ear patch; travels in busy flocks.
All-dark bulbul, red bill and legs; loud, gregarious, always overhead.
Dark blue, spangled; loud human-like whistle. Bounds along streams and wet rock.
Black + chestnut with white cap; flicks tail on boulders in rushing water.
Slate-blue male / grey female with rusty tail; constant on stream rocks.
Bulbul with short pale bill and pointed crest; olive-green, grey head.
Crested, brown with white nape collar; roving flocks.
Long down-curved bill; skulks low. More often heard than seen.
Tiny; male deep blue with orange throat. Perches quietly mid-storey.
Small, dark, star-spotted; hops on the forest floor at high elevation.
Tiny owl; false 'eye' spots on nape. Calls day and night — listen after dark.
Green with black-and-yellow head, blue crown; noisy foothill flocks.
Male white-backed with black underparts, red face; shy, flushes from trail.
Wild ancestor of the chicken; crows at dawn near village edges.
You WILL share the trail with these in the valleys. Give them space.
Common diurnal tree squirrel, reddish belly; chattering in canopy.
Squirrel-like but pointed snout; forages on the ground, quick and jittery.
Large; glides between trees. Look for eyeshine on the overnight leg.
Smaller glider, dark above/pale below; strictly nocturnal.
Long-bodied, facial stripe; nocturnal — best shot is headtorch eyeshine.
Stocky brown monkey in troops; wary of people.
Tiny burrowing insectivore found only here. Essentially never seen — bragging rights only.
You'll more likely hear the dawn song than see one. Critically endangered.
Goat-antelope of steep terrain; shy, mostly crepuscular.
Black with white chest crescent. Present but elusive — a lucky/uneasy sighting.
Robust stream frogs, spiny-chested males; night, in and beside cold streams.
Green/patterned frogs with big toe-pads; calling from wet vegetation after dark.
Warty, dark ridges on head; hops across damp trail at night.
Glossy small lizards darting off warm, sunny sections of trail.
Oversized head, long tail; hides in cool streams. Nocturnal and rare.
Aromatic conifer, flattened sprays of scale-leaves; prized, protected stands.
Whole stretches of trail tunnel through bamboo — a signature Sapa section.
Dominant broadleaf canopy of the montane belt; acorns underfoot.
Subalpine fir found only on the highest ridges here.
Old-growth conifer of upper slopes; drooping branchlets.
Trunked ferns with a crown of huge fronds; wet, shaded gullies.
Tall paddle-leaves, red-purple flower spike; clumps in warm valleys.
Leathery leaves; blazing red/pink blooms in spring (Sept = mostly foliage). Many species here.
300+ species, mostly epiphytes clinging to trunks and mossy branches. ID is hard on the move.
Succulent trailside herbs, spurred flowers; many endemic to these mountains.
Asymmetric fleshy leaves, pink/white flowers on dripping rock faces.
Climbing vine, 5-leaflet leaves; the famous local herbal 'immortality' tea.
Low understory herb of the ginseng family; heavily collected, now scarce.
You run straight through the terraces — golden at Sept harvest, mirror-flooded otherwise.
Waist-high glossy bushes on cultivated slopes near villages.
Large, tailed; gather to 'puddle' on damp mud and stream crossings in sun.
Huge black-and-gold butterfly; unmistakable slow glide in sunny clearings.

Bright leaf-green, triangular head, prehensile tail; coils motionless in low bushes and on branches at night — right where your hand reaches on a climb. Several northern species overlap (stejnegeri, gumprechti, albolabris).
notable: VENOMOUS - the encounter to plan for

field_notes: Slender, long-tailed, tan/brown with dark-edged blotches down the back; terrestrial to low shrubs, ambushes at night. Widely recorded across N. Vietnam mountains.
Stout, short-tailed, blotched brown; buries into leaf litter and ambushes. A true montane species of the north.
Camouflaged grey-brown with distinctive horn-like scales above each eye. Rare; specifically recorded at Sa Pa. A real sighting event.
Glossy, narrow white bands on black, rounded body, calm and sluggish by day. Nocturnal and terrestrial - overlaps your night leg in the warm valleys.
notable: HIGHLY VENOMOUS (neurotoxic) - among the most dangerous

field_notes: Bold black-and-yellow bands, triangular in cross-section with a ridged spine and blunt tail; slow, docile, nocturnal.
Rears and spreads a hood with an O-shaped mark when threatened; active dawn/dusk. Lower, warmer, cultivated sections.
Very long, olive-brown, narrow hood; can rear a third of its body. Shy and thinly spread - present but rarely met.
Small, metallic purple sheen, orange neck, pale jaw stripe. Described in 2023 from ~2,800 m on Fansipan by H'mong porters - a Hoang Lien signature.
notable: Rear-fanged (do not handle); Hoang Lien specialty

field_notes: Olive, checkered, with a red-orange patch on the neck; near rice and streams, active by day. Looks like a harmless grass snake.
notable: Rear-fanged but MEDICALLY SIGNIFICANT - not harmless

field_notes: Small, dark with pale bands - a convincing krait mimic; nocturnal, common around walls and trailsides. Treat any banded night snake as a krait until sure.
notable: Harmless (but easily mistaken for a krait)

field_notes: Large, fast, slender, olive to brown; diurnal, flees noisily through leaf litter when you pass.
Striking grey with black-ringed yellow diamonds; secretive, likes cool damp highland forest. A beautiful highland find.
Green (juveniles reddish) with vertical cat-like pupils; slender, arboreal, nocturnal.
Tiny, blunt-headed, big-eyed and slow; eats snails and slugs. Utterly harmless.
